{{Short description|Survey in the United Kingdom}}
[[File:Natsal-logo.svg|thumb]]
The '''National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles''' ('''Natsal''') is a series of surveys of people in the [[Great Britain]] regarding their sexual behaviour and patterns, and are among the largest scientific studies of sexual behaviours in the world.<ref>[https://www.ucl.ac.uk/global-health/national-surveys-sexual-attitudes-and-lifestyles-natsal National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, UCL.]</ref> The rounds of surveys completed to date are Natsal-1 (1990–1991) and Natsal-2 (2000–2001) and Natsal-3 (2010–2012), as well as Natsal-COVID (2020–2021).<ref>[https://www.natsal.ac.uk/natsal-surveys/ Natsal Surveys.]</ref> Data collection for Natsal-4 is taking place from September 2022 to December 2023.<ref>[https://natcen.ac.uk/our-research/research/natsal/ Natsal: The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles], National Centre for Survey Research.</ref> Natsal-4's Principal Co-investigators are Pam Sonnenberg and Cath Mercer, both professors at [[University College London|University College, London]].<ref>[https://www.natsal.ac.uk/about/natsal-team/meet-team/ Meet the Natsal team].</ref>

Natsal's findings are widely used in research and policy making, and have influenced public health policy in areas such as:
The National Sexual Health & HIV Strategy in England; the Scottish Sexual Health Strategy (2005-) and the Welsh Sexual Health Strategy, The Teenage Pregnancy Strategy (2000–2010), the National Chlamydia Screening Programme (NCSP), the national [[human papillomavirus]] (HPV) immunisation programme in 2008/9, the statutory provision of [[personal, social, health and economic education]] (PHSE) education in schools in 2009, Sexual health campaigns such as "Sex: worth talking about" in 2010, and the [[National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence]] (NICE) guidelines on long acting contraception (2006).<ref>[https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/research/centres-projects-groups/natsal#about About Natsal].</ref>

==History==
The first Natsal survey was carried out in 1990, in response to the urgent need of understanding sexual practices in the context of the [[Epidemiology of HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS epidemic]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/research/centres-projects-groups/natsal|title=National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) &#124; LSHTM|date=July 27, 2018|website=www.lshtm.ac.uk}}</ref> The Principal Investigator of Natsal-1, Natsal-2 and Natsal-3 was [[Anne Mandall Johnson|Anne Johnson]], a professor at University College, London,<ref>{{cite web |title=Survey examines changes in sexual behaviour and attitudes in Britain |url=http://www.wellcome.ac.uk/News/Media-office/Press-releases/2013/Press-releases/WTP054816.htm |website=www.wellcome.ac.uk |accessdate=2015-10-14}}</ref> and co-leader [[Kaye Wellings]], a professor at the [[London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lane|first=Richard|date=2013-11-30|title=Kaye Wellings: pioneering figure in sexual health|journal=The Lancet|language=English|volume=382|issue=9907|pages=1773|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(13)62346-6|pmid=24286783|s2cid=8753572|issn=0140-6736|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The Natsal-3 survey revealed, among other things, that British people are having sex less often than they did 20 years ago,<ref>{{cite news |title=Cambridge professor's in-depth analysis of sex survey reveals couples' secrets beneath the sheets |url=http://www.cambridge-news.co.uk/Cambridge-professor-s-depth-sex-survey-reveals/story-26249577-detail/story.html |accessdate=30 March 2015 |publisher=Cambridge News |date=29 March 2015}}</ref> but that same-sex experiences between women were growing more numerous.<ref>{{Cite news |title=How to conduct a sex survey |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/britain/2023/01/25/how-to-conduct-a-sex-survey |access-date=2023-01-26 |issn=0013-0613}}</ref>
